guide_sections.heading: Following the round trip through wide form
guide_sections.body:
The reference reshapes four measurements to wide form and back:

```text
long (4 rows)        wide (2 rows)              restored before cleanup
id visit value       row id value.1 value.2     row  id visit value
A  1     10          1   A  10      12          A.1  A  1     10
A  2     12          3   B  20      23          B.1  B  1     20
B  1     20                                     A.2  A  2     12
B  2     23                                     B.2  B  2     23
```

The wide table keeps row names 1 and 3, the rows where each id first appeared. Going back to long, reshape names each row from the id and the time, such as A.1, and lists all visit 1 rows before visit 2. Both directions also attach an attribute that records the reshape.

So the values survive the round trip, but `identical(restored, long)` would be FALSE for three reasons: row order, row names and the extra attribute. The reference sorts by id and visit, sets the row names to NULL, keeps only the three original columns and compares with `all.equal(..., check.attributes = FALSE)`. Each step removes a difference in bookkeeping, not in data.

exercises.approach: Name the cell key as id plus visit, and check it with `anyDuplicated(long[c("id", "visit")])`.
exercises.why: Each value belongs to one person at one visit. The four rows have four distinct pairs, so they fill the 2 by 2 grid of wide cells exactly once each.
exercises.wrong: Using id alone as the key. A appears twice and B appears twice, so the check would fail on correct data, and visit alone repeats in the same way.

exercises.approach: Add long rows for A and B at visit 3 and rerun the same reshape call.
exercises.why: reshape creates one value column per distinct visit, so a third visit becomes value.3, filled by matching on id. Both people have the visit, so the new column has no missing cells.
exercises.wrong: Appending a vector straight onto the wide table. Its values land by row position, and the order A then B exists only because of how the input happened to be sorted.

exercises.approach: Reshape back with varying value.1 and value.2, times 1 and 2, then sort by id and visit, drop row names and compare with all.equal ignoring attributes.
exercises.why: The values return unchanged, but reshape adds row names such as A.1 and a record of the reshape, and lists visit 1 rows first. Sorting and resetting removes those differences, leaving only the data to compare.
exercises.wrong: Comparing with `identical(restored, long)`. It returns FALSE because of row names, row order and the attribute, even though every measurement came back correctly.

exercises.approach: Check the key before reshaping, then reject the batch or apply a stated aggregation rule to the duplicate pair.
exercises.why: `rbind(long, long[1, ])` adds a second row for A at visit 1. A wide cell can hold one value, so without a rule reshape keeps the first and drops the other.
exercises.wrong: Reshaping anyway. The second value disappears with only a warning, so the wide table looks complete while missing a reading.
exercises.verify: `anyDuplicated(duplicate[c("id", "visit")])` returns 5, the position of the repeated row.

exercises.approach: Carry a presence flag in long form, one TRUE per recorded row, and reshape it alongside the value.
exercises.why: Removing B's visit 2 row leaves value.2 missing for B. A recorded row with value NA would look the same in wide form, so the value alone cannot tell absent from unknown.
exercises.wrong: Reading every NA in the wide table as a skipped visit. Some of those cells are recorded measurements whose value is unknown, and the visit counts come out wrong.
exercises.verify: `is.na(incomplete_wide$value.2[incomplete_wide$id == "B"])` returns TRUE, and the reshaped flag shows NA for the absent visit and TRUE for a recorded one.

exercises.approach: Choose the shape from the next operation: wide for a per person difference between visits, long for a chart or model with one row per measurement.
exercises.why: In wide form `value.2 - value.1` is 2 for A and 3 for B in one vectorized line. A chart with visit on the x axis needs visit as a column, which is the long layout.
exercises.wrong: Folding an aggregation into the reshape, such as averaging duplicates without saying so, and calling the result the same data.
exercises.verify: `wide$value.2 - wide$value.1` returns 2 and 3, and `nrow(long)` returns 4 measurements.
